description: Run linearity, time-invariance, causality and BIBO stability tests on eight example continuous-time systems. Each test overlays the two signals that the property says must be equal, reports whether they match, and explains the true classification of the system.

educational.topic: System properties: linearity, time-invariance, causality, stability and memory
learningObjectives: Explain the superposition principle and test a system for linearity
Distinguish time-invariant systems from time-varying systems using a shifted input
Determine whether a system is causal by comparing outputs for inputs that agree up to a given time
Classify a system as BIBO stable or unstable from its response to a bounded input

equations: Linearity: T[a x1 + b x2] = a T[x1] + b T[x2]
Causality: y(t0) depends only on x(t) for t <= t0
assumptions: Continuous-time systems are simulated on a 0.01 s grid from -8 s to 14 s and plotted from -2 s to 10 s
Property badges show the analytically known classification; the plotted comparison is one numerical example

keyQuestions: Why is y(t) = t x(t) linear but not time-invariant?
Which part of linearity does y(t) = x(t) + 1 violate?
Can a matching pair of curves prove that a system has a property?
commonMisconceptions: A system whose equation contains t multiplied by x(t) is nonlinear
Adding a constant to the input keeps a system linear
One passing example proves that a property holds
A system with a bounded output for one bounded input is BIBO stable
assessmentOpportunities: Fill in a property table for four systems before running the tests
Explain the maximum difference reported by the time-invariance test for y(t) = t x(t)
